terms.short: Highest price a buyer will pay
terms.definition: The highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay for a security.
examples: The bid on Infosys is ₹1,502, so that's where you can sell right now.
Bids dried up after the results and the stock gapped down.
terms.fill: To sell right away, you hit the ____.
wrong: The lowest price a seller will accept
The price of the last completed trade
The average price paid over the day
terms.note: Traders say they "hit the bid" when they sell at it.

tf.s: If you sell at market, you usually get the bid price.
tf.why: A market sell order hits the best bid.

terms.short: Lowest price a seller will take
terms.definition: The lowest price a seller is currently willing to accept. Also called the offer.
examples: Reliance is ₹2,850 bid, ₹2,851 offered.
We lifted the offer to get filled before the news.
terms.fill: To buy immediately, you pay the ____, the lowest price any seller is showing.
wrong: The highest price a buyer will pay
The price set by the exchange at the open
The difference between the bid and the offer
terms.note: Traders say they "lift the offer" when they buy at it.

terms.definition: The difference between the best bid and the best ask. A narrow spread means a stock is cheap to trade.
examples: The spread on this small cap is 40 bips, so getting in and out costs real money.
Spreads widen when volatility jumps.
terms.fill: Liquid large caps trade with a tight ____, so crossing from buyer's price to seller's price costs very little.
wrong: The daily range between the high and low price
The fee your broker charges per trade
The difference between today's close and yesterday's close

calcs.q: The bid is 100.10 and the ask is 100.30. What is the spread?

terms.definition: The price at which the most recent trade in a security happened. Indian apps and terminals show it as LTP.
examples: LTP is ₹845 but the bid is ₹844, so a market sell won't get ₹845.
terms.fill: The ____ shows where the latest deal happened, not where you can trade next.
wrong: The price at which the stock closed yesterday
The highest price of the day
The price the exchange fixes at the open

terms.definition: One hundredth of one percent (0.01%). Used for interest rates, spreads, costs and small returns.
examples: The RBI cut the repo rate by 25 bips.
We're paying 3 bips in brokerage on this order.
terms.fill: One ____ equals 0.01%, so 25 of them make a quarter of a percent.
wrong: One tenth of a percent
One percent of a company's shares
The smallest price step a stock can move

calcs.q: A bond yield rises from 6.85% to 7.10%. How many basis points is that?

terms.short: How easily you can trade without moving price
terms.definition: How easily you can buy or sell a security in size without moving its price much.
examples: Liquidity in midcaps dries up in a sell-off.
HDFC Bank has deep liquidity; you can trade large size without much impact.
terms.fill: Thin ____ means even a modest order can push the price sharply.
wrong: The cash a company holds on its balance sheet
The number of shares a company has issued
How much a stock's price swings in a day
terms.note: Volume and liquidity are related but not the same: a stock can trade a lot and still have thin order books.

terms.definition: The number of shares or contracts traded in a period, usually a day.
examples: Volume was three times the average on results day.
terms.fill: The breakout came on heavy ____, which traders read as conviction.
wrong: The total value of all shares of a company
The number of buy orders waiting in the book
The size of a fund's portfolio
terms.note: Turnover is volume in rupees: shares traded times price.

terms.definition: The total market value of a company's shares: share price times the number of shares outstanding.
examples: It's a ₹2,000 crore market cap company, so most large funds can't build a big position.
terms.fill: With 100 crore shares at ₹500 each, the company's ____ is ₹50,000 crore.
wrong: The total revenue a company earns in a year
The value of everything a company owns
The amount of money raised in an IPO

calcs.q: A company has 50 crore shares trading at ₹400. What is its market cap?

terms.short: Own it; gain if price rises
terms.definition: Holding a position that gains when the price rises, usually by owning the security.
examples: We're long HDFC Bank into the results.
Stay long, but tighten the stop.
terms.fill: If you own 1,000 shares of Infosys, you are ____ Infosys.
wrong: Holding a stock for more than a year
Betting that a price will fall
Having borrowed money to buy shares

terms.short: Positioned to gain if price falls
terms.definition: A position that gains when the price falls, usually by selling futures or selling shares you have borrowed.
examples: We're short the IT pack via futures ahead of the results.
terms.fill: A trader who expects the stock to fall can go ____ by selling its futures.
wrong: Holding a position for a short time only
Owning fewer shares than the benchmark
Selling a stock you already own
terms.note: In India, most traders go short with futures. Shorting cash shares overnight needs borrowed stock through securities lending (SLB); intraday shorts must be closed the same day.

tf.s: A short seller makes money when the price rises.
tf.why: A short makes money when the price falls.

terms.definition: The amount of a security you hold, long or short.
examples: We're building a position in Larsen over the next week.
Close out the position before expiry.
terms.fill: We bought 50,000 shares over three days to build our ____.
wrong: A stock's rank in an index
The price at which you plan to sell
Your place in the order queue

terms.definition: Profit and loss: how much money a trade, book or fund has made or lost.
examples: What's the P&L on the Bank Nifty trade?
The desk's P&L was down ₹2 crore on the day.
terms.fill: The trader checked the ____ at the close to see how much the book made today.
wrong: Price and liquidity
A statement of what a company owns and owes
The limit on how much a trader can lose

terms.definition: Profit or loss on positions you have already closed. It is final.
examples: Realised P&L is ₹4 lakh; the rest is still open.
terms.fill: Once you sell the shares, the gain becomes ____ and no longer moves with the price.
wrong: Profit you expect to make by the end of the year
Profit on open positions at today's prices
Profit after paying tax
terms.note: Traders often call it "booked" profit: "we booked profits in metals."

terms.short: Gain or loss on open positions
terms.definition: Profit or loss on positions you still hold, valued at current prices. It keeps changing until you close the position.
examples: We're up ₹10 lakh unrealised, but nothing's booked yet.
terms.fill: The stock rallied, but we haven't sold, so the gain is still ____ and could vanish tomorrow.
wrong: Profit that has been paid out as a dividend
Profit on closed trades
Loss that the broker has written off

tf.s: Unrealised P&L becomes realised only when you close the position.

terms.definition: Valuing positions at current market prices, usually every day. In futures, MTM gains and losses are settled in cash daily.
examples: MTM losses on the futures have to be paid in by tomorrow.
terms.fill: Futures positions are ____ every day, and any losses are taken from your margin.
wrong: Valuing positions at the price you bought them
Selling all positions at the end of the day
Marking a stock as risky on the exchange

terms.short: Gain or loss as a percentage
terms.definition: The gain or loss on an investment, usually shown as a percentage of the amount invested.
examples: The fund's one-year return is 18%.
terms.fill: Bought at ₹100, sold at ₹120: that's a 20% ____.
wrong: Cash a company pays back through buybacks
Getting your money back when an order is cancelled
The interest rate set by the RBI

terms.definition: Compound annual growth rate: the steady yearly rate that would take a starting value to an ending value over several years.
examples: Earnings grew at a 15% CAGR over five years.
terms.fill: Money that roughly doubles in 6 years has grown at about a 12% ____.
wrong: The total return over the whole period
The simple average of each year's return
The growth in a company's share count

calcs.q: An investment grows from ₹1 lakh to ₹2 lakh in 6 years. Its CAGR is closest to?
calcs.why: Doubling in 6 years is about 12% a year (2^(1/6) ≈ 1.12). The rule of 72 gives 72 ÷ 6 = 12. 16.7% is the simple average, which ignores compounding.

terms.definition: A payment a company makes to its shareholders out of profits, usually in cash.
examples: The board declared an interim dividend; the record date is next Friday.
terms.fill: Mature companies like utilities often pay out a large share of their profits as a ____.
wrong: Interest paid on a company's bonds
Extra shares given free to shareholders
The profit a trader makes on a stock

terms.definition: Annual dividends per share divided by the share price, shown as a percentage.
examples: At ₹400 with a ₹20 dividend, the yield is 5%.
terms.fill: A ₹10 annual dividend on a ₹200 stock is a 5% ____.
wrong: The total dividend a company pays in rupees
Dividends as a share of company profits
How fast dividends grow each year
terms.formula: annual dividend per share ÷ share price

calcs.q: A stock at ₹500 pays ₹15 of dividends a year. What is its dividend yield?

terms.definition: The full return on an investment, including both price change and income such as dividends, assuming the income is reinvested.
examples: The index was up 10%, but total return was 11.3% with dividends.
terms.fill: To compare a high-dividend stock fairly with a growth stock, look at ____, not price change alone.
wrong: Return before costs and taxes
Return since the stock first listed
The return of the whole market

calcs.q: You buy at ₹200, sell at ₹230 and received a ₹4 dividend along the way. What is your total return?

terms.definition: The total value a derivative or leveraged position controls, as opposed to the cash put up for it.
examples: The futures position is ₹5 crore notional, but we've only posted ₹80 lakh of margin.
terms.fill: We only posted margin, but the ____ of the futures position is several times bigger.
wrong: The cash you deposit with your broker
The value of a position after fees
The price at which an option can be exercised

calcs.q: You buy futures on 300 shares of a stock at ₹1,000. What is the notional value?

terms.definition: Controlling a position larger than your own capital, through borrowing or derivatives. It magnifies both gains and losses.
examples: At 5x leverage, a 4% move against you wipes out 20% of your capital.
terms.fill: Futures give you ____, so a small price move makes a big dent in your capital.
wrong: Spreading money across many stocks to reduce risk
Negotiating lower brokerage with your broker
Holding cash to protect against a fall

calcs.q: You put up ₹2 lakh of margin to hold a ₹10 lakh position. The position rises 3%. What is the return on your margin?
calcs.why: 3% of ₹10 lakh is ₹30,000, which is 15% of ₹2 lakh. Leverage of 5× turns 3% into 15%.

terms.definition: Indian unit for one hundred thousand, written 1,00,000. Ten lakh make one million.
examples: The minimum ticket size for the PMS is ₹50 lakh.
wrong: One million (10,00,000)
Ten thousand (10,000)
Ten million (1,00,00,000)

calcs.q: ₹25 lakh is how much in millions?

terms.definition: Indian unit for ten million, written 1,00,00,000. 100 crore make one billion.
examples: The block was ₹1,200 crore, or 12 billion rupees.
terms.fill: ₹100 ____ equals one billion rupees.
wrong: One hundred thousand (1,00,000)
One billion (100,00,00,000)
One million (10,00,000)
terms.note: Global investors think in millions and billions: ₹1 lakh crore is ₹1 trillion.

calcs.q: How many lakh make one crore?

terms.definition: The plain difference between two percentages. A move from 10% to 12% is 2 percentage points, even though it is a 20% increase.
examples: Promoter holding fell 3 percentage points to 51%.
terms.fill: If a bank's bad-loan ratio goes from 4% to 5%, it has risen by one ____.
wrong: One hundredth of a percent
A percentage change relative to the starting value
A point on the Nifty or Sensex

calcs.q: A loan rate goes from 8% to 10%. That's 2 percentage points. How much higher is it in percent terms?

tf.s: A rate going from 4% to 5% is a 1% rise.
tf.why: It is a 1 percentage point rise, which is 25% in relative terms.

terms.short: Nominal value printed on a share
terms.definition: The nominal value of a share set by the company, such as ₹1, ₹2 or ₹10. It has little to do with the market price, but Indian companies often announce dividends as a percentage of it.
examples: A 200% dividend on a ₹1 face value share is just ₹2 per share.
terms.fill: A "500% dividend" sounds huge, but on a ₹2 ____ share it is only ₹10.
wrong: The current market price of a share
The company's net worth per share
The price at which a share was first sold in the IPO

terms.short: Net worth on the balance sheet
terms.definition: A company's net worth on its balance sheet: assets minus liabilities. Book value per share divides it by the number of shares.
examples: Several PSU banks traded below book value for years.
terms.fill: When a bank trades at less than its ____, the market values it below its accounting net worth.
wrong: The total value of the company's shares on the market
The nominal value printed on a share
The value of a stock according to analysts' targets

terms.definition: Trading above a reference value, such as fair value, NAV, the issue price or the price in another market. The opposite of a discount.
examples: The stock listed at a 40% premium to its IPO price.
terms.fill: The ETF is trading above its NAV, so buyers are paying a ____.
wrong: The fee paid to a broker
A bonus share given to long-term holders
Trading below a reference value
terms.note: In options, "premium" also means the price you pay for the option.

terms.definition: Trading below a reference value, such as NAV, fair value or the price in another market. The opposite of a premium.
examples: The holding company trades at a 50% discount to the value of its stakes.
terms.fill: The QIP was priced at a 5% ____ to the market price to attract big investors.
wrong: A rebate on brokerage
The interest rate a central bank charges
Trading above a reference value

terms.short: Estimate of what it's really worth
terms.definition: An estimate of what an asset is really worth, from a valuation model or pricing formula, compared with its market price.
examples: Our fair value for the stock is ₹1,400, so we see 20% upside.
terms.fill: Analysts compare the market price with their estimate of ____ to decide if a stock is cheap.
wrong: The price agreed between two friends
A price fixed by SEBI for every IPO
The average price over the last year

terms.definition: How much a price could rise from here, usually to an analyst's target. Downside is the potential fall.
examples: We see 25% upside to our target of ₹900.
terms.fill: With the stock at ₹800 and a target of ₹1,000, there's 25% ____.
wrong: The profit already made on a position
How much a stock rose yesterday
The maximum loss on a trade

terms.definition: Earnings per share: a company's net profit divided by its number of shares.
examples: EPS grew 18% year on year.
terms.fill: Net profit of ₹500 crore spread over 100 crore shares gives an ____ of ₹5.
wrong: Expected price of the share next year
Dividend paid per share
Revenue divided by the number of shares

terms.definition: Share price divided by earnings per share. It shows how many rupees investors pay for each rupee of yearly profit.
examples: The stock trades at 40 times earnings, so expectations are high.
terms.fill: At ₹600 a share and EPS of ₹30, the stock's ____ is 20.
wrong: Profit divided by revenue
Price divided by book value per share
Price divided by dividend per share

calcs.q: A stock trades at ₹900 and its earnings per share are ₹45. What is its P/E?

terms.short: Share price ÷ book value per share
terms.definition: Share price divided by book value per share. Widely used to value banks and other financial companies.
examples: The bank trades at 1.2 times book.
terms.fill: Banks are often valued on ____, since their assets are mostly loans carried close to book value.
wrong: Price divided by earnings per share
Profit divided by book value
Price divided by sales per share
terms.formula: share price ÷ book value per share

terms.definition: The value of the whole business to all its investors: market cap plus debt minus cash.
examples: On EV to EBITDA, the telecom stock looks cheap despite all the debt.
terms.fill: To compare companies with very different debt levels, analysts use ____ rather than market cap.
wrong: Market cap minus debt
The value of a company's factories and equipment
The expected value of next year's earnings

calcs.q: Market cap ₹10,000 crore, debt ₹3,000 crore, cash ₹1,000 crore. What is the enterprise value?

terms.definition: Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. A rough measure of a business's operating profit.
examples: EBITDA margin expanded 200 bips on lower raw material costs.
terms.fill: Analysts value capital-heavy businesses on EV to ____, which ignores how they are financed.
wrong: Profit after all expenses and taxes
Total revenue before costs
Cash paid out to shareholders

terms.definition: A valuation ratio such as P/E or EV/EBITDA. "Trading at 30x" means 30 times earnings or another base.
examples: The sector re-rated; multiples expanded from 25x to 35x.
terms.fill: When investors turn more optimistic, a stock's ____ expands even if its earnings don't change.
wrong: The number of times a stock has split
How many times a share has doubled
The leverage a trader is using

terms.definition: A company's profit, usually net profit, reported every quarter. Results season is when most companies report.
examples: Earnings beat estimates by 8%.
terms.fill: Stocks often move sharply when quarterly ____ come in above or below estimates.
wrong: A company's total sales
Salaries paid to employees
Cash raised from investors
terms.note: Indian companies mostly use an April to March financial year, so Q1 is April to June.

terms.definition: A company's own forecast of its future results, such as revenue growth or margins.
examples: Management cut revenue guidance to 4–6%, and the stock fell 7%.
terms.fill: The IT company raised its full-year ____, signalling demand is better than feared.
wrong: Advice from a broker on what to buy
Rules from SEBI on disclosure
The average of analysts' forecasts

terms.definition: The average of analysts' forecasts for a company's results or an economic number. Results are judged as a beat or a miss against it.
examples: Profit came in 5% below consensus.
terms.fill: Results are called a "beat" when they come in above ____.
wrong: A company's own forecast
Agreement among board members
An official target set by the exchange

terms.short: What it's worth; how it's priced
terms.definition: What a company or asset is worth, or how expensive it is compared with its earnings, assets or peers.
examples: Valuations look stretched after the rally.
terms.fill: After a 60% rally, many investors worry that the stock's ____ is no longer cheap.
wrong: The number of shares a company issues
The audit of a company's accounts
The rating given by a credit agency

terms.definition: A position taken to reduce the risk of another position, such as selling Nifty futures against a stock portfolio.
examples: We hedged the portfolio with Nifty puts into the budget.
terms.fill: To protect the portfolio from a market fall without selling stocks, the PM put on a ____ with index futures.
wrong: A bet that magnifies gains
A type of high-risk stock
A limit on how much a trader can buy

terms.definition: Spreading money across different stocks, sectors or assets so that one bad outcome doesn't sink the portfolio.
examples: Ten bank stocks isn't diversification; it's one bet.
terms.fill: Holding stocks from many unrelated sectors is a form of ____.
wrong: Buying more of a stock as it falls
Using futures to cancel out risk exactly
Splitting a stock into more shares

tf.s: Owning 30 stocks from the same sector gives good diversification.
tf.why: They share the same sector risk, so they tend to fall together.

terms.short: All the holdings of an investor or fund
terms.definition: The full set of investments held by a person or a fund.
examples: The portfolio has 40 stocks with a tilt to financials.
terms.fill: The fund manager reviews the whole ____ every week, not just single stocks.
wrong: A single large holding
A folder of company reports
The list of stocks in an index

terms.short: Index a fund is measured against
terms.definition: The index or yardstick a fund's performance is compared with, such as the Nifty 50 for a large-cap fund.
examples: We beat the benchmark by 3% this year.
terms.fill: A large-cap fund that returned 14% while the Nifty 50 returned 12% beat its ____ by 2 points.
wrong: The minimum investment for a fund
The highest price a stock reached this year
A SEBI rule on fund fees

terms.definition: To deliver a higher return than a benchmark or peers. As an analyst rating, it means the stock is expected to beat the market.
examples: Pharma outperformed the Nifty by 6% this quarter.
terms.fill: Our bank stocks rose 15% while the bank index rose 10%, so we managed to ____ the index.
wrong: To trade more often than others
To make any profit at all
To fall less than expected

terms.definition: To deliver a lower return than a benchmark or peers, even if the return itself is positive.
examples: IT has underperformed the market for two years.
terms.fill: Gaining 8% when the benchmark gains 12% means you ____ it by 4 points.
wrong: To lose money
To trade less than usual
To miss an earnings estimate

terms.short: How much is riding on something
terms.definition: How much of a portfolio is affected by a particular stock, sector, factor or market, in rupees or as a percentage of the portfolio.
examples: Our banking exposure is 30% of the fund.
terms.fill: With 30% in banks, the fund has heavy ____ to interest rate moves.
wrong: Publicity a company gets in the media
The total fees a fund charges
The time left until a contract expires

terms.definition: How much and how fast a price moves up and down. Higher volatility means bigger swings and more risk.
examples: Volatility spiked ahead of the election results.
terms.fill: Small caps can swing 5% in a day, so their ____ is much higher than that of large caps.
wrong: How many shares trade in a day
How quickly a company grows
The gap between the bid and the ask

terms.definition: A broad group of investments that behave in similar ways, such as equities, bonds, commodities, real estate or cash.
examples: Gold was the best-performing asset class this year.
terms.fill: Equities, bonds and gold are each a different ____.
wrong: A ranking of stocks by quality
The class of shares that carry voting rights
A group of stocks in one sector
